title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks
claim: A slow feedback variable reshapes the energy landscape so a stable state loses stability and the system escapes to the next one.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, aligned to a bottom time axis with arrows
description: Three rounded gray panels run left to right. Each panel is a 1-D energy landscape drawn as a black curve, with dashed vertical lines marking memories ξ1 and ξ2. Arrows from each panel point down to a horizontal time axis with ticks at 0, an unlabeled middle point, and T_esc. In the first panel a red ball rests in the ξ1 well. In the middle panel, green text reads 'slow variable z action, κ > κ_crit'. A green up arrow sits over the ξ1 well and a down arrow over the ξ2 well. Faded gray curves show the ξ1 well becoming shallower and the ξ2 well deepening, and the red ball is shown at several fading positions. In the third panel the ξ1 well has become a hill, the ball has rolled off it, and the ξ2 well is now the deep minimum. The eye goes first to the red ball and the green arrows.
caption: Schematic illustration of the proposed two-timescale mechanism for sequential memory transitions. At the initial time, the fast state variable is at a stable equilibrium corresponding to memory ξ1. The slow variable z progressively destabilizes this equilibrium while simultaneously stabilizing the equilibrium associated with memory ξ2. At the escape time Tesc, the equilibrium corresponding to ξ1 loses stability and the system transitions toward ξ2. This transition occurs only when the gain parameter κ of the slow dynamics exceeds a critical threshold κcrit. We analytically characterize both κcrit and the resulting escape time Tesc.
abstract: Associative memory models classically describe retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but the theory of sequential retrieval remains comparatively limited. We develop a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network in which fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. This yields autonomous, graph-constrained transitions while preserving analytical tractability. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, we characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify the geometric regions that govern stability loss and escape from retrieved memories. We further derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse, expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points. Together, these results provide a tractable framework for analyzing feedback-driven sequential retrieval in Hopfield networks.
